Volume 13 · Chapter 10

Mechanism design and auctions

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v13-c09

By the endDerive incentive-compatible allocation and payment rules with explicit informational assumptions.

Volume 13 · Chapter 10

Mechanism design and auctions

An auctioneer can change who wins, what losing bidders owe, when a bidder may decline, and which information a payment uses. Those choices affect incentives before they affect revenue. A public authority may choose an efficient project and still need external resources to pay its contractor. A platform may sell to the highest value and yet earn less than a mechanism that sometimes favors a lower value. To evaluate a design, specify the information, rights and accounts before optimizing its receipts.

Capability. Construct a direct mechanism from a selected equilibrium; prove Groves truthfulness and its qualified participation guarantee; derive allocation/payment characterizations including jumps; prove a global optimal-auction theorem in a stated independent private-value class; and distinguish revenue equivalence from claims that survive a change in preferences. Six original cases and twelve fully solved exercises develop these results from explicit primitives.

Prerequisites. Static games and refinements supplies mixed strategies, conditional Bayesian best replies and the distinction between an equilibrium and its selection. Information economics and screening supplies pairwise IC inequalities, integral envelopes and transfer-integrability cautions. Contracts and dynamic incentives supplies commitment, hidden-action and participation distinctions. The introductory Auctions and matching and Public goods and common resources provide continuity; the present proofs do not assume that introductory uniform-price examples establish the graduate results.

All values, distributions, costs and cash endowments below are original instructional assumptions, not estimates or legal rules. Payments are in units of a single numeraire. Buyers privately know their own values; the designer can enforce the announced allocation and transfers. Unless expressly changed, agents are risk neutral, communication is costless, the population is fixed, and wealth or borrowing does not constrain any allowed payment. Participation is evaluated at the stated date. A favorable model calculation does not establish these conditions in a real procurement or platform.

1. Implementation: which deviations are being reproduced?

Agent i observes type θi. An indirect mechanism has message sets Mi and a committed rule g mapping messages and its announced random seed to an outcome. An outcome includes physical allocation and all payments. Utility ui(o,θi) depends on the agent’s true type, not on the label it reports. A strategy σi(θi) is a message or a distribution of messages. A direct mechanism instead asks each agent to report a type. Dominant-strategy incentive compatibility (DSIC) means that truth is a best reply at every fixed vector of opponents’ reports. Bayesian incentive compatibility (BIC) means that truth is a best reply after averaging opponents’ truthful strategies under the conditional law given the agent’s true type. All IC inequalities here are weak: truthful play may tie another report.

First take finite type, message and outcome sets, so all expectations are finite sums. For the continuous cases, use Borel spaces and measurable strategy/outcome kernels; assume absolute integrability for every evaluated type/report deviation and ex ante payoffs, and specify a regular conditional type law for every type at which BIC is asserted. An almost-everywhere equilibrium assertion yields only an almost-everywhere conclusion unless its null types are separately completed. Mixed strategies use independent private seeds, with the mechanism’s public randomization stated separately. We are not silently adding a correlating mediator to an originally independent-strategy game. Hidden actions or message costs with direct utility effects would have to be included in the reproduced outcome; they are absent in this theorem.

Dominant-strategy revelation theorem. Suppose σ is a selected dominant-strategy equilibrium of the original mechanism. Define the direct rule: on report profile r, draw a message mi according to σi(ri) for each agent, then run g on those messages. This is a rule the designer commits to, not a claim that agents voluntarily obey an instruction after they have sent messages.

Proof. Fix i’s true type θi and any vector r−i. In the original game, σi(θi) is at least as good as the feasible alternative message distribution σi(ri) against every fixed opponent-message profile. Integrating that inequality over the independent messages drawn from σ−i(r−i) and the original mechanism coins preserves it. Its left and right sides are exactly the direct utilities from reporting θi and ri. Thus the direct mechanism is DSIC, in expected utility over its coins. Truth at every type profile reproduces the original selected outcome distribution. A mixture of false reports cannot do better because it averages inequalities already proved for each report. No claim of truthfulness for each realized random seed follows unless the underlying comparisons also hold seed by seed.

Bayesian revelation theorem. Suppose instead that σ is a selected Bayes–Nash equilibrium for a specified joint type law. Use the same direct rule. Conditional on the true θi, a false report ri simulates precisely the feasible original strategy deviation σi(ri). Opponents’ types retain their actual conditional law given θi, and their simulated messages retain the original conditional distribution. The original Bayesian best-reply inequality therefore gives the direct truthful inequality after taking those same expectations. Mixed false reports are again covered by integration. At truth the entire selected outcome distribution is reproduced. Independence of types is unnecessary for this composition proof; replacing the true conditional law by the posterior associated with the false report would be an error.

A direct IC mechanism itself is an implementing mechanism, so these constructions justify searching over direct mechanisms when the objective depends only on the reproduced allocation/payments and the same participation constraints. They establish selected-equilibrium implementation. They do not say that every equilibrium is truthful, that the implementation is unique, that hidden actions become verifiable, or that communication and enforcement are free in practice. Exercise 1 makes the distinction concrete: composing a Bayesian first-price equilibrium gives BIC while leaving profitable deviations at particular opponents’ reports.

Method route: Ozdaglar, Mechanism Design II, slides 4–6 and 18–19, states the two revelation principles and distinguishes their inequalities. The strategy-composition proofs and the randomization/integrability qualifications above are supplied here.

2. Efficient transfers and the designer’s resource account

Let Ω be a finite nonempty feasible outcome set. Agent i has a finite real valuation vi(ω,θi), potentially a vector rather than a single number. The designer incurs a known report-independent real resource cost C(ω). An outside numeraire account can finance this cost. Payment pi flows from agent i to the designer, so utility is vi−pi and designer net receipts are Σpi−C. There is commitment, no binding payment budget and no unmodeled externality in an agent’s utility. Choose a reported-welfare maximizer, breaking ties using a fixed ordering of Ω independent of the reports:

ω*(r)∈argmaxω∈Ω{Σjvj(ω,rj)−C(ω)};
pi(r)=hi(r−i)−[Σj≠ivj(ω*(r),rj)−C(ω*(r))].

Each hi can be any finite function of opponents’ reports alone. Groves truthfulness proof. Fix opponents’ reports. If i reports truthfully, its utility equals the maximized expression with its own true valuation and others’ reported valuations, minus the report-independent hi. A false report merely selects some other feasible ω; it cannot make that true-own/reported-others expression exceed its global maximum. This proves DSIC without differentiability or a prior. The cost appears once in the maximized welfare and once in the bracket defining each agent’s payment; it is not multiplied by the number of agents in the physical resource ledger.

Pivot normalization and individual rationality. Define a without-i environment Ω−i, and let hi be the maximum of others’ reported welfare net of the designer’s cost there. Assume every such outcome can be embedded in Ω with the same others’ values and cost and nonnegative value for i. In an excludable assignment this added value is zero; in a public project a removed payer may still enjoy a nonnegative benefit. The full optimum’s welfare is at least hi, by considering an embedded without-i optimum. Therefore truthful utility, full welfare minus hi, is nonnegative when the outside option is normalized to zero. This proves ex-post IR against truthful opponents under the stated embedding. It does not follow from the word “pivot” if exclusion changes feasibility, imposes a cost on i, or leaves an outside option with higher utility.

Transfers cancel in the consolidated identity Σ(vi−pi)+(Σpi−C)=Σvi−C. DSIC, participation and efficiency do not by themselves imply that Σpi covers C. Negative payments are allowed by the general formula; their feasibility would need funding too. The next two cases calculate actual receipts and resources, not just an incentive inequality.

Worked case 1. Two delivery slots and a multi-parameter pivot

A seller can allocate distinct goods A and B, at most one to each of three unit-demand buyers. It may retain either good. The values, with rows identifying buyers, are ((9,4),(8,7),(3,6)). A delivered good costs the seller 1 in real resources. Retention costs zero. Buyers have zero value if unassigned, and sufficient numeraire to pay any allowed charge. The without-i problem retains both goods and simply removes i. There are 13 feasible full assignments: no sale, six one-good allocations and six two-good allocations to distinct buyers.

The efficient choice is A→1, B→2, yielding gross value 9+7=16, cost two and welfare 14. A→2, B→3 yields only 12 net; A→1, B→3 yields 13. Enumerating the remaining assignments also gives at most 14. Without buyer 1, allocate A→2 and B→3 for welfare 12; without buyer 2, allocate A→1 and B→3 for 13; without buyer 3 the full allocation remains feasible for 14. Hence the pivot constants are (12,13,14).

At the chosen allocation, others’ values net of the same cost two are 5, 7 and 14. Payments are therefore (7,6,0), and buyer utilities are (2,1,0). Receipts, resource cost and seller net receipts are (13,2,11). Buyer utility three plus seller net receipts eleven equals welfare fourteen. Delivery cost is not charged again as a second loss after this reconciliation.

As a transfer, allow delivery of A only. Buyer 1 wins with net social value eight; removing it makes buyer 2’s value eight, net of cost one, the best alternative. Buyer 1 pays 8, obtains utility one, and seller net receipts are seven. Total surplus is 8. This is the second-price threshold in this restricted environment. The two-good result is a multi-parameter welfare mechanism, not a claim that its revenue is maximal among mechanisms.

Worked case 2. An efficient public project with a funded deficit

A project has real cost 12 and nonnegative private benefits (7,6,4). Its feasible outcomes are build or do not build, with zero cost/benefits for no build. Build at a reported-sum tie with cost. Removing a payer leaves the project technologically possible and leaves others’ benefits unchanged. The removed person’s full-economy benefit is nonnegative, so the embedding condition holds. Write S−i for the sum of other reported benefits and y for the build decision. Pivot payments are

pi=max(0,S−i−12)−(S−i−12)y.

The project is built because total benefit is 17. The other-benefit sums are 10, 11 and 13. Thus payments are (2,1,0), utilities are (5,5,4), and revenue is three. Buyer 3 is not pivotal for the build decision and pays zero; this does not mean its benefit is zero. The mechanism’s receipts fall short of cost by 9. Social surplus is 5.

Specify the financing: before any reports, the designer has irreversibly committed 12 units of its own numeraire to the project account. It collects the three payment units before paying the contractor twelve, and closes with 3. Its wealth change is −9, not +3. Buyer utility fourteen plus that wealth change equals surplus five. The financing is an actual endowed account; it is not a free balancing transfer or evidence that VCG funds itself. This example disproves automatic self-financing. It does not prove a universal impossibility theorem about every efficient incentive-compatible public-good mechanism.

Method route: Ozdaglar, slides 7–12. Those slides use transfers to agents; this chapter consistently uses payments from agents and explicitly includes known designer costs. No general Groves-necessity or budget-balance impossibility result is imported.

3. Payments determined by allocation, including jumps

Now agent i’s private scalar value lies in [0,Hi], with Hi finite and positive. Its expected allocation xi is in [0,1], and payment pi is finite; utility is vixi−pi. At a fixed vector of opponents’ reports, suppress their notation and set U(v)=vx(v)−p(v). If the rule randomizes, x and p are expectations over its coins. No density assumption is needed for this pointwise characterization.

Necessity. For v<w, truth at w gives U(w)≥U(v)+(w−v)x(v), while truth at v gives U(w)≤U(v)+(w−v)x(w). Therefore x(v)≤x(w), and

(w−v)x(v)≤U(w)−U(v)≤(w−v)x(w).

Partition [0,v] and sum the bounds on every adjacent interval. The resulting lower and upper Riemann sums surround U(v)−U(0). Their difference is at most the partition mesh times x(v)−x(0), hence tends to zero. Bounded monotone x is Riemann integrable, including any jumps and endpoint values. Consequently

U(v)=U(0)+∫0vx(s)ds,   p(v)=vx(v)−∫0vx(s)ds−U(0).

Sufficiency. Start with any nondecreasing x and this payment. For v<w, the integral of x over [v,w] lies between (w−v)x(v) and (w−v)x(w). These are exactly the two IC inequalities. Every pair is covered, including a report at a jump, and mixtures of reports cannot improve expected utility. Thus the characterization is necessary and sufficient. Since x≥0, the minimum truthful utility is U(0); IR for every type at this fixed opponent profile holds exactly when U(0)≥0. A specified allocation determines payments only after specifying that constant, which may depend on opponents’ reports.

For a deterministic threshold allocation with U(0)=0, every unserved bidder pays zero and every served bidder pays the threshold. At the equality type either allocation is allowed; utility is zero under both. More general expected allocations need not specify a unique realized payment lottery or realized IR. The theorem is DSIC in expected monetary utility over the mechanism’s announced randomization at every fixed opponent-report profile.

Worked case 3. A price lottery and an interim-only truth-telling rule

A single buyer has v∈[0,10]. Offer allocation zero for v<2, one third for 2≤v<7, and one for v≥7, with normalized U(0)=0. The two thresholds and lower positive probability are (2,7,1/3). Integrating the step allocation gives expected payments (0,2/3,16/3) on those three regions. Utilities are respectively 0, (v−2)/3 and v−16/3. At v=5, the allocation/payment/utility triple is (1/3,2/3,1); at v=7 it is (1,16/3,5/3). The utility is continuous at seven even though allocation and payment jump.

A stronger implementation draws a posted price of two with probability one third and seven with probability two thirds, independently of the report. The buyer receives the object and pays the drawn price exactly when its report weakly exceeds that price. Truth is optimal for each realized price: accept precisely when value covers payment, with acceptance selected at equality. Thus this implementation is truthful and IR for every seed. At v=5, the payment conditional on winning is two, while the unconditional expected payment is two thirds. The envelope alone would not guarantee these realized properties for an arbitrary payment lottery with the same mean.

For a contrast, take two agents with independent types zero or two, each equally likely. Their values and fair marginals are ((0,2),(1/2,1/2)). Allocate one object by a fair coin independent of both reports ri∈{0,2}. Set p1=(r1−1)(r2−1) and p2=−p1. Each agent has at least one unit of numeraire, so the transfers of magnitude one are feasible and balance exactly; the designer needs no net cash. Before seeing the other type, either report has expected payment zero. Each true type therefore obtains interim utility θ/2 and truth is a weak Bayesian best reply. This is BIC and interim IR.

It is not DSIC or ex-post IR. If agent 1’s true type is zero and the other report is zero, truth requires payment one, whereas reporting two receives one. Allocation is unchanged, so the lie gains 2. Some low-type truthful realizations have negative utility. Participation must be committed at the interim date; adding a later rejection right changes the mechanism. Independence made these report-contingent transfers average to zero. Exercise 5 holds the marginals fixed and changes dependence, reversing the truthful comparison.

4. From interim incentives to a global revenue bound

For the rest of this section, values are independent with known distributions on [0,Hi]. A mechanism specifies jointly measurable expected allocations xi(r)∈[0,1] with Σxi(r)≤1, and payments. Each report’s payment has finite absolute expectation against opponents/coins, and ex ante absolute payments are integrable. These are separate requirements: per-report integrability alone would not ensure that revenue exists after integrating a continuum of true types. Values and allocations are bounded. Define Xi(ri)=E−ixi(ri,V−i) and Pi similarly.

Interim characterization. Independence ensures that the same law of V−i applies whether the true type is v or w. Hence BIC says exactly vX(v)−P(v)≥vX(r)−P(r) for all v,r. Apply the complete pairwise/Riemann proof from section 3 to X and P: BIC is equivalent to nondecreasing X and P(v)=vX(v)−∫0vX(s)ds−U(0). Interim IR for every type is U(0)≥0. This does not say that every collection of monotone interim allocations can be implemented jointly; an underlying ex-post feasible mechanism remains part of the domain. Under correlated types, a false report is evaluated against the law conditional on the true type, so the common-law reduction need not hold. The basic Bayesian revelation proof did not require this extra independence assumption.

Assume each Fi is absolutely continuous, with a positive density on the interior of its support. Endpoints of zero probability can be treated directly by the integral formula. Using the envelope, and reversing the bounded nonnegative rent integral, yields

E[Pi(Vi)] = ∫0HᵢvXi(v)fi(v)dv − ∫0Hᵢ∫0vXi(s)ds fi(v)dv − Ui(0)
=∫0Hᵢ[vfi(v)−(1−Fi(v))]Xi(v)dv−Ui(0)
=E[φi(Vi)xi(V)]−Ui(0),   φi(v)=v−(1−Fi(v))/fi(v).

The first interchange is justified by boundedness and Tonelli for the nonnegative rent term. The weighted expression vf−(1−F) is absolutely integrable on a bounded interval, so the signed virtual identity is legitimate. Independence identifies E[φX] with E[φx]. Never substitute an endpoint where f=0 into the ratio; the preceding integral remains meaningful. A regular law here means that its virtual value has a nondecreasing version on the interior; assume a nondecreasing endpoint extension, possibly with an infinite negative lower limit, for the allocation rule. Endpoint extensions are used only for allocation ranking. The revenue identity and virtual-product bound below are evaluated on interior profiles, which have probability one; an expression such as (−∞)·0 is never used. Endpoint payments are defined by the allocation integral, not a virtual-value product. The examples needing this theorem have finite linear virtual values.

Optimal-auction theorem. Let the seller’s value and delivery cost be zero. Among all the measurable, integrable, ex-post feasible BIC mechanisms satisfying interim IR for every type, revenue is bounded by E[max(0,φ1(V1),…,φn(Vn))]. Indeed Ui(0)≥0, and for every profile with finite defined interior virtual values, hence almost surely, nonnegative allocations summing to at most one satisfy Σφixi≤max(0,φ1,…,φn). Integrate this pointwise upper bound and use the identity. This bounds every feasible Bayesian design in the declared class; it is not just a first-order comparison among reserve prices.

Attainment and proof of incentives. Assign the object to a highest nonnegative virtual value, with a fixed report-independent priority among ties, and do not sell if every virtual value is negative. At virtual value zero, select a sale using that same priority. Regularity implies each buyer’s allocation is nondecreasing in its report: raising its virtual value cannot turn a winner into a loser against fixed rivals. Section 3 constructs normalized payments and proves DSIC and IR; for binary allocation they are critical values on winning and zero on losing. The construction attains the pointwise bound almost surely and has Ui(0)=0, proving global optimality against the stated BIC/interim-IR class. Weak plateaus can leave multiple optimal designs; no uniqueness is claimed. With iid strictly increasing virtual values, ranking virtual and physical values agrees, and the rule is second price with reserve threshold r=inf{v:φ(v)≥0}. At the threshold itself, eligibility follows the stated virtual-value/boundary convention; the critical payment remains r. This threshold is a zero when a zero exists, but strict monotonicity alone does not exclude a jump across zero. With asymmetric laws, the ranks can differ.

If delivering costs a known c≥0 only when the object is allocated, replace the objective by net receipts E[Σpi−cΣxi]. The same proof bounds it by E[max(0,φ1−c,…,φn−c)], attained by assigning to the highest virtual value at least c and using its critical payment. Gross receipts and net profit are distinct. Unknown costs, irregular virtual values, budget constraints, interdependent values and endogenous entry require additional analysis; no ironing or general multi-object revenue theorem has been proved here.

Worked case 4. A lower physical value can win the optimal auction

Two independent values are uniform on [0,6] and [0,12], respectively; their upper endpoints are (6,12), and the seller has zero value/cost. Their virtual values are 2v1−6 and 2v2−12. They are strictly increasing. Bidder 1 wins when v1≥3 and v2≤v1+3; bidder 2 wins when v2≥6 and v1<v2−3, subject to bidder 1’s fixed tie priority. No sale occurs when both virtual values are negative. Winning payments are max(3,v2−3) for bidder 1 and max(6,v1+3) for bidder 2; losers pay zero. At values (5,7), virtual values are (4,2), so bidder 1 wins and pays 4, with utility one. Allocating instead to value seven would maximize that profile’s gross value, not its virtual surplus.

Let Z=max(0,φ1,φ2). For 0≤t≤6, independence gives Pr(Z>t)=1−((t+6)/12)((t+12)/24)=(216−18t−t²)/288. For 6≤t≤12, the first bidder cannot exceed t, so Pr(Z>t)=(12−t)/24. Integrating these two polynomial tails yields revenue

E[Z]=∫06(216−18t−t²)/288 dt+∫612(12−t)/24 dt=31/8.

An independent receipts calculation integrates actual critical prices. With joint density 1/72, bidder 1 pays three on v2∈[0,6], v1∈[3,6], and pays v2−3 on v2∈[6,9], v1∈[v2−3,6]. Bidder 2 pays six on v1∈[0,3], v2∈[6,12], and pays v1+3 on v1∈[3,6], v2∈[v1+3,12]. These regions give expected payments (1,23/8), reconciling exactly with 31/8.

No sale requires v1<3 and v2<6, which has probability one quarter. Sale probability is 3/4. Integrating the winner’s physical value over the same regions gives parts (23/16,65/16), hence expected allocated value 11/2 and buyer rent 13/8. The efficient allocation has E[max(V1,V2)]=13/2; its ordinary second-price revenue is E[min(V1,V2)]=5/2. Thus optimal revenue rises while expected total surplus falls by 1. This is a model-specific comparison with known priors, not an empirical recommendation.

Method route: Roughgarden, Revenue-Maximizing Auctions, sections 1.3–3.1. The source’s differentiable payment calculation is replaced above by a jump-valid proof. Its brief extension to all BIC mechanisms is established here by the interim identity and the pointwise feasible upper bound.

5. Revenue equivalence and full equilibrium verification

Conditional revenue-equivalence theorem. Suppose two BIC mechanisms operate under the same independent private-value law and quasilinear preferences. If they give each type the same interim allocation Xi(v) and the same bottom utility Ui(0), their interim payment functions agree, because both equal vXi(v)−∫0vXi(s)ds−Ui(0). Integrating gives the same expected revenue when absolute transfers are integrable. This is an immediate consequence of the proved characterization; it is not a statement that all auctions have the same revenue. A change in reserve, participation, information, preferences, allocation or bottom rent can invalidate the comparison.

If losers pay zero, P(v)=X(v)E[payment | win,v]. It is the unconditional interim P that the envelope identifies. When X(v)=0, a conditional winning payment need not be defined. If losers also pay, include (1−X(v))E[payment | lose,v] as well. An all-pay auction is a useful warning: its unconditional payment is its bid, whereas in first price it is the bid times the winning probability.

Worked case 5. A nonuniform law, three auctions, and global deviations

Three bidders have iid values with F(v)=(v/10)², 0≤v≤10; n=3. Bids are any finite nonnegative numbers. Highest bid wins with a fixed priority for ties; continuous equilibrium values make interior ties have probability zero. In first price only the winner pays its own bid. In all pay everyone pays its own bid. In second price the winner pays the highest other bid. Losers otherwise pay zero. Values are private; monetary utility is linear; the seller commits and bidders can finance all allowed payments. The highest rival type has CDF G(v)=F(v)²=(v/10)4.

The efficient interim allocation is X(v)=G(v). Normalize bottom utility to zero. Direct integration gives

U(v)=v⁵/(5·10⁴),   P(v)=4v⁵/(5·10⁴);
bFP(v)=P(v)/G(v)=4v/5  (v>0),   bFP(0)=0,   bAP(v)=P(v).

Although f(v)=v/50 is positive for v>0, f(0)=0. These expressions come from the allocation/payment integral, not a virtual-value ratio at zero. An envelope-derived candidate is not yet an equilibrium; verify all deviations.

First-price sufficiency. Against opponents bidding 4v/5, any bid in [0,8] corresponds to an imitated type z∈[0,10]. True type v obtains (v−4z/5)(z/10)4. Its derivative in z is 4z³(v−z)/10⁴. It is nonnegative below z=v and nonpositive above, so z=v globally maximizes on [0,10], including v=0 and v=10. Bids above eight win with probability one but pay more than eight and hence cannot beat the bid-eight payoff, already compared. Bid zero has zero expected payoff except on null all-zero rival types and is covered by the boundary. This proves a symmetric BNE over the full nonnegative bid domain, not just a first-order condition or a local optimum.

All-pay sufficiency. The candidate bid map 4z⁵/(5·10⁴) increases continuously from zero to eight, so every bid in [0,8] is represented. True type v’s payoff is v(z/10)4−4z⁵/(5·10⁴), whose derivative is again 4z³(v−z)/10⁴. The same sign argument gives the global optimum z=v. Bids above eight only increase the certain payment at a winning probability already equal to one. Thus the all-pay strategy is also a symmetric BNE. Its interim utility is nonnegative, but a positive-value bidder who loses pays a positive bid and obtains negative realized utility. Interim participation must be enforceable; this is not realized ex-post IR.

Second-price truthfulness. Fix the highest rival bid m. Winning yields monetary gain v−m, losing yields zero. A truthful bid wins when v>m and loses when v<m; at equality both give zero, regardless of tie priority. No other bid improves this statewise monetary payoff. Hence truth is dominant; its efficient allocation and zero bottom utility match the two constructed Bayesian equilibria. No uniqueness claim about all equilibria of these games is needed.

At v=5, first-price bid, winning probability, interim payment and utility are (4,1/16,1/4,1/16). The all-pay bid is one quarter, not four. Conditional on winning, the first-price payment is four; multiplying by 1/16 gives the correct interim payment. The expected maximum value is 60/7, because its CDF is (v/10)6. Expected revenue in each format is 48/7; aggregate rent is 12/7, and each bidder’s ex ante utility is 4/7.

These receipts can also be calculated without using the equivalence conclusion. First-price receipts are four fifths of the winning value, giving (4/5)(60/7). All-pay receipts integrate the three bids against f(v)=v/50: 3∫010[4v⁵/(5·10⁴)](v/50)dv=48/7. The second-highest value has density 12v³/10⁴−12v⁵/10⁶; integrating v times that density also gives 48/7. The three independent accounts agree with the theorem because its assumptions agree, not because the payment rules coincide in each realization.

Method route: Levin, Auction Theory, October 2004, pages 3–7. Page 6 correctly derives the interim integral but then omits the winning-probability factor when identifying it with a conditional order-statistic expectation. The distinction P(v)=X(v)·conditional winning payment is retained here; the complete bid-domain sufficiency arguments are supplied independently.

6. Changing utility changes the incentive problem

Worked case 6. A strict, globally defined preference counterexample

Keep the value law, independent opponents, allocation, payments and bid domain of worked case 5. Change only each bidder’s utility of monetary gain z to u(z)=1−2^(−5z), z∈ℝ. This CARA function is increasing and strictly concave on the entire real line, including negative overbid gains. Normalize u(0)=0. We test whether the old profile b(v)=4v/5 remains an equilibrium; we do not assume a new equilibrium formula.

A type five bidding four wins with probability 1/16, makes gain one on winning and zero otherwise. Its expected utility is 31/512. A bid of 24/5 beats opponents whose types are below six, winning with probability (6/10)4=81/625. Its monetary winning gain is 1/5, whose utility is one half. Expected utility is therefore 81/1250. The strict improvement is 1361/320000. Expected monetary gains instead are (1/16,81/3125), so the new preference rewards the higher winning probability despite a lower expected monetary gain.

The difference between this fixed deviating bid’s expected utility and the old candidate’s expected utility is a continuous function of the true value around five. It is strictly positive at five, so it remains positive on some open interval contained in (0,10). The density there is positive; thus a positive-probability set of types can improve. This refutes a Bayesian equilibrium assertion even if optimality were required only almost everywhere. A single isolated profitable type would not have been enough for that claim.

Truthful second-price bidding remains dominant under this increasing utility: the statewise monetary payoff comparison from case 5 is preserved by any increasing transformation u, and averaging preserves it. This statement does not determine the new first-price equilibrium or compare its revenue with second price. The risk-neutral envelope used money-linear utilities and therefore cannot simply be reused for the new first-price problem. Exercise 11 derives the local direction of failure for a larger strictly concave class without pretending to solve that class’s equilibrium.

Research and implementation workflow. Specify who knows each variable, which distribution is maintained, what the seller can commit to, what happens after a refusal or default, and who finances negative transfers or resource costs. Establish all best replies, not only candidate first-order conditions. Reconcile physical surplus, payments and each account. Then ask whether the data identify private values or only selected bids, whether participation and preferences transport to a new rule, and whether the stated equilibrium is the one an institution would select. An exact numerical optimum cannot answer those information and enforcement questions.

Reproduce the cases. Enumerate the thirteen assignments using exact rational values, solve each removal problem, and reconstruct the transfers from welfare differences. For the auction integrals, split the stated winning regions at each threshold and integrate the polynomial prices and physical values separately. The displayed fractions can be checked with the Python standard library’s fractions.Fraction. Editorial checks also test changed laws, costs, participation constants, malformed domains and the full derivative certificates. A finite bid grid would be inadequate evidence for the global incentive claims, whose analytic proofs are given above.

7. Exercises: prove the contract before comparing receipts

Use the stated payment sign and tie conventions. Unless a problem changes them, inherit the relevant worked case’s complete information, funding and participation assumptions. All twelve questions have solutions below. Exercise 12 is an open research critique with an explicit ten-point rubric; the others have determinate calculations or proof obligations.

  1. Construct the direct mechanism that simulates the selected first-price equilibrium in case 5 from reported types. Prove BIC by composition and calculate the type-five interim allocation, payment and utility. At opponents’ reports (2,3), compare true type five’s reports five and four. Does the revelation construction prove DSIC or unique implementation? State where independence is and is not used.
  2. In the two-good case, change only buyer 3’s value of B from six to 8. Enumerate the relevant full and removal optima. Find the allocation, payments, utilities, receipts, cost, seller net receipts and total surplus. Explain why the known delivery cost belongs in both the welfare comparison and the resource account without being counted twice.
  3. Keep public-project cost twelve and designer opening cash twelve, but change benefits to (8,3,2). Calculate pivot payments, utilities, deficit, surplus and closing cash. A proposal instead charges each agent four whenever the reported total reaches twelve. Show an actual profitable report deviation under this proposal and assess truthful participation.
  4. A buyer’s report selects acceptance of a posted price three with probability one quarter and eight with probability three quarters. The independent draw is fixed before report comparison and equality selects acceptance. Use type support [0,10] and normalized bottom utility. Derive x, p and U on every region, including equality reports, and compute the allocation/payment/utility triples at values six and nine. Explain what is unique in the envelope result and what stronger feature this implementation has.
  5. Keep the fair allocation and transfer formula of the two-agent side-bet example, but use the joint law on (0,0),(0,2),(2,0),(2,2) given by (3/8,1/8,1/8,3/8). Show that the marginal type distributions are unchanged. Compute agent 1’s truthful and opposite-report conditional expected payments for each own type. Is the original truthful profile BIC under this law? Explain the correct conditional law for a lie.
  6. In the asymmetric optimal auction, calculate the winner, payment and utility at ((4,8),(6,9)). At the second profile, consider a true type-nine bidder 2 reporting slightly more than nine. Reconcile its changed allocation with IC, and identify the role of the fixed tie priority.
  7. For two iid uniform values on [0,8] and zero seller value/cost, derive the globally revenue-optimal BIC/interim-IR rule. Compute its reserve, sale probability, revenue, expected allocated value and buyer rent. Compare with the efficient zero-reserve second-price auction. The argument must bound all feasible BIC mechanisms, not merely differentiate a one-dimensional reserve formula.
  8. Return to case 4’s unequal supports but charge the seller a known real delivery cost 2 exactly when a sale occurs. Maximize net receipts. Derive the allocation and critical payments; compute sale probability, each bidder’s expected payment, total gross receipts, expected cost and net profit. Prove global optimality in the declared class and keep gross and net objectives separate.
  9. In the power-distribution case, reduce the number of independent bidders to 2 and keep F(v)=(v/10)². Derive symmetric first-price and all-pay bids and verify global best replies over all nonnegative bids. Calculate the type-five first-price bid, winning probability, interim payment and utility, plus expected maximum, revenue and total rent.
  10. Add a compulsory fee 2/7 to each of the three participants in every case-5 format, regardless of report or outcome. In the fixed-population committed game, find total revenue, aggregate buyer utility and bottom utility; assess incentive comparisons and IR. Explain why making this fee voluntary at an earlier entry stage prevents mechanically reusing the fixed-three-bidder calculation.
  11. Let u be differentiable, strictly concave and increasing on ℝ, with u(0)=0. Against the case-5 risk-neutral opponents b(z)=4z/5, differentiate a true type v’s first-price expected utility from imitating z. Show the derivative at z=v is strictly positive for every v∈(0,10), using a supporting-tangent argument. State exactly what this establishes and what it does not establish about a new equilibrium.
  12. A report claims: “Revelation makes truth the only equilibrium; efficient VCG pays for any public project; first price and all pay must collect the same amount after preferences or entry change; and the best reserve in a tested grid proves the optimal auction.” Write a short referee response correcting each claim with a proof condition or counterexample from this chapter. Propose a feasible evidence and implementation audit for a real auction redesign, and identify what an observed bid distribution alone fails to establish. Use the scoring guide below.
Solutions, proofs and evaluation criteria

  1. On reports r, simulate bids 4ri/5, allocate to the highest simulated bid and charge the winner its simulated bid. With other agents reporting truthfully, any false report is an available original first-price bid; the original global Bayesian best-reply proof therefore gives truth a weak Bayesian best reply. More generally the section-1 composition integrates against the conditional law of rivals given the true type, so it requires no independence by itself. Independence is used in case 5 to derive the specific rival CDF and equilibrium. Type five’s interim triple is (1/16,1/4,1/16).

    At rivals’ reports two and three, the largest rival simulated bid is 12/5. Reporting five pays four and yields utility one. Reporting four pays 16/5 and still wins, giving utility 9/5 and gain 4/5. The direct mechanism is thus not DSIC. The revelation theorem copies a selected equilibrium’s distribution and permits weak ties/other equilibria; it does not prove unique or full implementation. All reports remain within [0,10] and their simulated bids are feasible.

  2. A→1 and B→3 give gross value seventeen and net welfare fifteen. Alternatives A→1/B→2 and A→2/B→3 give fourteen net, while the other two-good and all one-good assignments are lower. Removal of buyer 1 gives A→2/B→3 and welfare fourteen; removal of buyer 2 leaves the full optimum at fifteen; removal of buyer 3 gives A→1/B→2 and welfare fourteen. Thus the constants are (14,15,14). At the full allocation, the others’ net values are six, fifteen and seven, so payments are (8,0,7). Utilities are (1,0,1). Receipts, cost and seller net receipts are (15,2,13); the latter plus utility two equals surplus 15. Costs determine which alternative is efficient and enter each agent’s externality comparison. In the physical ledger exactly two units are spent, once. Payments redistribute the remaining value; they are not additional resource costs.

  3. Benefits total thirteen, so build. The others’ sums five, ten and eleven are all below twelve; removing any agent prevents building. Payments are (7,2,1), utilities (1,1,1), receipts ten and deficit 2. Surplus is 1. Opening designer cash twelve plus receipts ten minus contractor payment twelve closes at 10; its wealth loss two plus buyer utility three equals surplus one.

    With equal fees four, the true type-two agent gets −2 from a truthful build. Reporting zero makes the total eleven, produces no build and payment zero, and increases utility by 2. The type-three agent also has negative truthful utility. The equal-fee rule balances the resource budget conditional on building, but violates the stipulated IC and truthful IR conditions. Neither the pivot deficit nor this particular failure proves a universal impossibility theorem.

  4. For v<3, (x,p,U)=(0,0,0). For 3≤v<8, x=1/4, p=3/4 and U=(v−3)/4. For v≥8, x=1, p=3/4+6=27/4 and U=v−27/4. Equality types accept the matching drawn price and are indifferent about that realization; utility remains continuous. The three expected payment levels are (0,3/4,27/4). The type-six triple is (1/4,3/4,3/4), and the type-nine triple is (1,27/4,9/4). The pairwise/Riemann proof establishes every report inequality without differentiating at three or eight. Given x and U(0), the expected payment is unique, but its realized distribution is not. This independent posted-price implementation is truthful and IR at every seed because the buyer accepts a particular price exactly when value covers it. That stronger property is not implied for an arbitrary mean-preserving payment lottery.

  5. Each marginal is (1/2,1/2), but the conditional probability that the other type matches one’s own is 3/4. For true type zero, truthful r1=0 pays +1 when r2=0 and −1 when r2=2, so its conditional expected payment is 1/2; reporting two reverses the signs and gives −1/2. For true type two the matching/high event again has probability 3/4, and the same pair of means results. Thus truthful and opposite-report payments are (1/2,−1/2) for either type, and agent 1 gains 1 by lying. Allocation remains one half, so this disproves BIC for the profile. There is no need for both agents to have a profitable deviation. The posterior used for the lie remains conditional on the agent’s true information, not the falsely announced type. Equal marginals do not preserve the interim common-law property.

  6. At (4,8), virtuals are two and four, so bidder 2 wins and pays max(6,4+3)=7, with utility one. At (6,9), virtuals are both six. Fixed priority assigns to bidder 1, whose critical price is max(3,9−3)=6, giving zero utility. Bidder 2 loses at truth with zero utility; a report slightly above nine wins but pays the critical value nine, so its true utility remains 0. IC is weak and permits this indifference. The report-independent priority specifies the allocation at an equality point while preserving monotonicity and the threshold payment; a winning probability can change without a strict utility improvement.

  7. The virtual value is 2v−8. The feasible pointwise upper bound is max(0,2v1−8,2v2−8), and normalized critical payments attain it by the theorem. Thus the optimal reserve is 4, the winner is the highest value at least four, and the price is the greater of four and the other value. This proves optimality against every feasible BIC/interim-IR rule in the stated class. Both values are below four with probability one quarter, so sale probability is 3/4.

    For the maximum M with density m/32 on [0,8], expected virtual revenue is ∫48(2m−8)m/32 dm=10/3. Expected allocated value is ∫48m²/32 dm=14/3, leaving buyer rent 4/3. With zero reserve, sale occurs surely except on a null all-zero profile, revenue is the expected minimum 8/3, and allocated value is the expected maximum 16/3. Buyer rent is 8/3. Raising the reserve excludes some positive-surplus trades, increases receipts and lowers buyer rent.

  8. Maximize positive virtual value net of cost two. Bidder 1 must have v1≥4 and v2≤v1+3; bidder 2 must have v2≥7 and outrank bidder 1’s virtual value. Retain priority 1 on ties. Critical payments are max(4,v2−3) and max(7,v1+3), respectively; losers pay zero. The pointwise bound max(0,φ1−2,φ2−2), together with the normalized envelope and IR, proves global net-profit optimality. Gross-receipt maximization alone would not subtract the resource cost.

    No sale has probability (4/6)(7/12)=7/18, so sale probability is 11/18. Bidder 1’s payment integral is [∫074(6−4)dv2+∫79(v2−3)(9−v2)dv2]/72=49/54. Bidder 2’s is [∫047(12−7)dv1+∫46(v1+3)(9−v1)dv1]/72=305/108. Thus expected payments are (49/54,305/108), gross receipts 403/108, expected real cost 11/9, and net profit 271/108. These regions independently reconcile actual payments with the expected virtual-profit identity.

  9. The highest opponent value now has CDF G(v)=(v/10)². The envelope gives U(v)=v³/(3·10²), P(v)=2v³/(3·10²), first-price bid 2v/3 and all-pay bid P(v). For first price, a bid in [0,20/3] corresponds to z∈[0,10] and gives (v−2z/3)(z/10)²; its derivative is 2z(v−z)/10². All pay gives v(z/10)²−2z³/(3·10²) with the same derivative. Both functions rise then fall around z=v. Bids above 20/3 cannot improve on that upper endpoint because the winning probability is already one and the payment rises; zero and endpoint types are included. This verifies the constructed equilibria globally.

    For type five, the first-price bid/winning probability/interim payment/utility tuple is (10/3,1/4,5/6,5/12). The maximum has CDF (v/10)4, hence expected value 8. Revenue is 16/3, either by two-thirds of that maximum or by direct all-pay integration. Total rent is 8/3. Changing competition changes allocation probabilities and rents even though the individual type law is unchanged.

  10. Because the fee is independent of every report, it cancels from all within-game report/bid comparisons; the same selected equilibria remain in the compulsory fixed-population games. Revenue becomes 54/7, aggregate buyer utility 6/7, and each bottom type’s utility −2/7. The allocation is unchanged, but the boundary constant changes, so the original no-fee payment identity cannot be reused with U(0)=0. Low enough types violate interim IR, including zero. A voluntary earlier entry decision changes who participates and opponents’ conditional type distributions, possibly the number of rivals and bid functions. An entry equilibrium and its funding/participation rules must be solved before predicting receipts. The fixed-three-bidder arithmetic is not a revenue forecast for that different game.

  11. At any z near an interior v, utility is (z/10)4u(v−4z/5), because losing gives u(0)=0. Differentiation gives [4z³u(v−4z/5)−(4/5)z⁴u′(v−4z/5)]/10⁴. At z=v this is

    (4v³/10⁴)[u(v/5)−(v/5)u′(v/5)].

    For s=v/5>0, strict concavity and differentiability imply u(0)<u(s)+u′(s)(0−s). To see strictness, equality of a supporting line at distinct points would force affinity on their interval, contradicting strict concavity. Since u(0)=0, the bracket is positive; the remaining factor is positive. A small increase in z remains inside [0,10] and strictly improves expected utility, so the risk-neutral candidate fails at every interior type. This is a best-reply direction against the old opponents, not a complete symmetric risk-averse equilibrium solution. It supplies no general revenue ranking of the newly solved first-price auction, whose existence and bidding function have not been derived here.

  12. Ten-point rubric. Award two points for correctly limiting revelation to a selected equilibrium and mapping false reports to feasible original deviations; exercise 1 disproves DSIC for a direct Bayesian implementation and nothing forces unique truth. Award two points for the known-cost welfare/transfer comparison and the actual endowed project ledger: case 2 needs nine units of designer wealth, despite efficiency and DSIC, and is a particular deficit example rather than a universal impossibility proof. Award two points for naming the shared allocation, money-linear preferences, independent common comparison law, boundary utilities and fixed participation population behind revenue equivalence; cases 6 and exercise 10 identify two concrete failures when those assumptions change. Award two points for the global BIC/IR virtual upper bound plus an implementable attaining allocation/payment rule; a reserve grid or first-order condition checks only a restricted family and does not prove the theorem.

    Award the final two points for a specific evidence and execution plan with an honest limit. A credible answer could propose a preannounced pilot with audited random assignment of comparable lots to enforceable rules, bidder information and eligibility held fixed where feasible, records of bids, winning payments, losing payments, actual delivery costs, cash guarantees, participation and defaults. It should explain how interference, entry selection, changing beliefs and repeated participation affect the interpretation. Observed bid distributions alone do not reveal private values without an equilibrium/information model, identify risk preferences, verify commitment, or establish that an alternate rule would select the same behavior. An excellent answer states which condition each observation can test and which counterfactual requires further identification or bounds. A mechanically balanced spreadsheet or good in-sample bid fit is insufficient evidence for universal implementation or optimality. Different justified pilots may receive full credit; no specific policy recommendation is required.

8. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to a colleague why an efficient mechanism can require a funded deficit, why revenue optimization may select a lower-valued buyer, and why a truthful direct mechanism can still permit other equilibria. A complete explanation connects the first to the difference between a Groves welfare comparison and the designer’s cash account; the second to the interim rent cost encoded in a known prior’s virtual value; and the third to equilibrium composition, which reproduces one selected strategy distribution without eliminating alternatives. Use the project’s nine-unit wealth loss and the (5,7) allocation as concrete checks.

Delayed retention, without looking back. Derive monotonicity from the two cross-report inequalities. Explain how the proof survives an allocation jump. State what fixes the additive payment constant, and which information assumption permits the interim version. For a winner-only payment, distinguish P(v) from its conditional winning price. Finally, state why the CARA calculation refutes an almost-everywhere equilibrium claim.

Answer key. Summing the two IC inequalities gives (w−v)(x(w)−x(v))≥0. Adjacent inequalities summed over fine partitions squeeze utility increments between Riemann sums, so jumps do not require differentiability. U(0), equivalently a bottom participation normalization, fixes the payment constant. Independence makes opponents’ law common across true types and false reports for the one-variable interim characterization, although basic Bayesian revelation itself does not need it. Winner-only P equals winning probability times conditional price; all-pay requires the losing-payment term too. The CARA improvement is strict and continuous around an interior value where the density is positive, so an open set of types gains.

The next chapter, Matching, networks and market design, changes the feasible allocation and deviation structure. Before carrying over a transfer-based theorem, identify whether payments are permitted, whether agents can block an allocation as a coalition, and whether network position changes feasible trades. A matching or network design is not automatically a single-item auction with more labels.
